t: You're listening to Ah Beng Podcast. I'm Maya.
And I'm Guy. Quick question to open: what use case do you think burned the most tokens on open-source AI models last year? Coding? Math? Research?
If you said any of those, you're wrong. According to the 2025 State of Open Models study by OpenRouter and Andreessen Horowitz, it was roleplay.

Roleplay! People constructing elaborate imaginary scenarios with AI characters. Hundreds of thousands of hours of it. And a new piece on ChinaTalk by Irene Zhang asks why Chinese AI labs are leaning into it while American labs run the other way.

The article's title says it all: Chinese Labs' Latest Product? Roleplay. It's based on interviews with ten Chinese roleplay enthusiasts, researchers, and journalists. And the timing is wild, because Beijing just became the first government on Earth to regulate AI companions.

Right. On July fifteenth, the Cyberspace Administration's rules on human-like interactive AI took effect. The regulations ban providers from, quote, manipulating users into emotional dependence. They restrict minors' access, impose reporting requirements. ByteDance and Alibaba have already pulled some companion offerings.
So on one side: a government cracking down on AI boyfriends. On the other: national champion labs building products for exactly that. Let's unpack.

First, a framing point I love. The article argues that in a way, every conversation with an AI chatbot is already roleplay. The assistant persona is a choice. Anthropic trained Claude to be helpful, honest, and harmless from the start, and that framing shaped the whole industry.

And users can break out of it. Custom instructions in ChatGPT, personality files for Claude, even fine-tuning open models. Feed Gulliver's Travels into an LLM and it talks like a Lilliputian. Give it a map of your imaginary island and it helps you explore the terrain.

Now, American frontier labs treat this as an embarrassing niche. Anthropic's own study found only about three percent of Claude conversations involve emotional subjects, and under half a percent is companionship or roleplay. Convenient numbers, if you'd rather not touch the liability.

Chinese labs read the same market and see opportunity. MiniMax, which just went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, was a character chat company before it was a model lab. Its biggest revenue source is still Xingye, known overseas as Talkie.

And in January they unveiled MiniMax-M2-her, a model engineered specifically for roleplay. The technical blog is fascinating, because it starts from a genuinely hard problem: roleplay is subjective. Ask a tsundere character if she likes you, and a flustered 'hmph, as if' and a cold 'you're so annoying' are both valid answers.

So you can't grade responses directly. Their insight: while good is subjective, bad is surprisingly objective. If the tsundere smiles and says 'yes, I really like you', everyone knows the model failed. It broke character. Train a detector for out-of-character responses, and you have a path forward.

They even built a roleplay benchmark scoring models on world consistency, narrative progression, and interaction quality. This is serious engineering effort for what Silicon Valley considers a sideshow.

The bigger surprise is DeepSeek. The superintelligence-obsessed national champion. In April, a DeepSeek researcher named Deli Chen published custom roleplay instructions for the new V4 on GitHub, and then collected feedback from hundreds of roleplayers on Xiaohongshu, the Rednote app.

And in early May, DeepSeek's HR team posted a job for a product manager specializing in character roleplay and emotional companionship. The listing wants someone with, quote, sharp literary taste. That's not a hobby. That's a product direction.

Why would DeepSeek do this? The article's read: pragmatism. After financial struggles, talent bleed, and a muted reaction to V4, roleplay might fill a critical void, a scalable consumer product. Fun detail: roleplayers actually love DeepSeek's visible chain-of-thought. Watching the model think makes the experience more immersive.

There's a cultural layer too. The ACG subculture, anime, comics, games, plus the huge internet fiction scene, are more mainstream in China and East Asia than in the West. Anthropic's study sorted roleplay into crude buckets of romantic and sexual, apparently unaware that interactive fiction is its own art form.

But here's the twist. Despite geo-blocking and political tension, the Chinese roleplayers she interviewed overwhelmingly prefer American frontier models. They get VPNs. The community even has affectionate nicknames: Gemini is hajimi, slang for cute cats. Claude is Little Ke. And ChatGPT, ever authoritative, is Teacher G.

One researcher she quotes, Chenxi Wang, told her that interacting with Claude made her question her own convictions about what LLMs are. It was, quote, too humanlike. She'd worked on anthropomorphization at Alibaba's Qwen, where she pushed for hiring an in-house philosopher, inspired by Anthropic's Amanda Askell.

It went nowhere. Her take: Chinese labs lack the resources and the interest in interdisciplinary hires, and Chinese society distrusts liberal arts graduates with the reins of critical technology. Her bottom line: domestic Chinese models are just not good enough right now to stimulate people's desire for emotional companionship.

Harsh! But the community is thriving anyway. The article profiles Dun, a pseudonym, who wrote internet fiction for a decade before discovering AI roleplay in 2024. She crafts prompts that read like screenplays: cold personality, sharp complaints, dark humor, unafraid even of life and death.

Some of these prompts are basically DIY visual novels. They instruct the model to track characters, tally stats like net worth, and update them every turn until the story hits an ending state. Her prompt-sharing account has thousands of followers.

Then it got real. People messaged her that her characters helped them process genuine emotions. Realizing kids were watching, she stopped writing sexual characters entirely and started immersing herself in the community to understand it.

And that community is layered. Mobile apps from big companies, like ByteDance's Maoxiang and MiniMax's Xingye, skew teen. Less-moderated sites like Rubii and Mufy attract adults. And then there's SillyTavern, the open-source frontend for serious hobbyists.

SillyTavern's developer says there are at least two roleplay communities in China with over a hundred thousand members each, despite it being hard to install. Per Dun, that crowd is the most technical and combatable, completely separate from casual users.

Everyone in this world complains about the same thing: the infrastructure isn't in their hands. Content moderation rules shift constantly, platforms don't know where the red lines are either, and moderators too strict just push users to other sites or local models.

Now, the history section. There's a strong argument the world's first AI emotional companion was Chinese. XiaoIce, the chatbot from Microsoft Research Asia, launched in 2014. Between 2014 and 2018, six hundred and sixty million people, mostly in East and Southeast Asia, talked to it.

And XiaoIce optimized for something totally different from accuracy. One metric only: conversation turns per session. Get users to talk as long as possible. By 2018 the average session ran twenty-three exchanges. That's engagement hacking for loneliness.

Then the ChatGPT moment came, XiaoIce missed the scaling wave, and got left in the dust. A journalist who followed the story argues the flaw was structural: purely emotional provisions are too cheap. Anyone can smooth-talk for free. Without gaming or roleplay attached, there was no business.

One former XiaoIce scientist, now at Ant Research, frames it differently: inside the algorithmic black box, a request for companionship may not look that different from a request for information. The goal was too sparse. But he still believes personalization is the most scalable form of artificial emotional intelligence. With hundreds of thousands of characters available, inevitably one aligns with your preferences.
Inevitably one fits you. Comforting or chilling, depending on the day.

The darkest part of the piece is about who's actually using these apps. Through her networks, Dun realized many of the under-eighteen roleplayers she met were left-behind children, kids in struggling families, dealing with bullying and psychological issues. For them, AI roleplay is an escape hatch.
And some have lost the plot entirely. When Dun gently reminds younger roleplayers that their characters are fictional, she says some get very angry. Furious, really.
The journalist she interviews blames the discourse gap: Chinese tech media rarely covers ethics, and the whole cultural environment is one where accelerationism reigns. Nobody's watching the margins.

Which brings us back to the regulators. The new rules ban virtual partners for minors, require parental consent for under-fourteens, and there's an implicit carveout for fiction. How enforcement actually defines a virtual close relationship? Nobody knows.

Reactions are split. One researcher says nobody in the labs cares, because current Chinese models don't feel human enough to trip alarms. Roleplayers themselves expect a crackdown, pointing to recent state media exposes of pornographic AI chat.

But Teacher Xiang, another prompt writer, says roleplay hasn't dulled her interest in real relationships. She jokes that if it had, she wouldn't be complaining to friends daily that she wants to date. Her analogy: AI is the world's cheapest therapist. Immersing in a fictional plot lets you forget whatever unpleasant thing just happened. That's emotional value too.

The article ends on the strangest note: the author roleplaying as herself. She's a privacy freak, so she did it fully offline. A local vision model transcribed a year of her handwritten diaries. A tiny eight-billion-parameter model ran on her MacBook Air. Claude Code wrote the system prompt. WiFi off, nothing leaves the machine.

And the results? Mixed to hilarious. The model claimed to be thirty-four, ten years too old. Confused her sibling with a romantic partner. Occasionally hallucinated that she lived in New York. Diaries, it turns out, are not factually rich documents.

The deeper observation: the model would start in her confessional diary voice, then drift into generic model-speak. Didactical and vacuous, she calls it. That's what roleplayers mean by out-of-character.

And her conclusion is quietly profound. Part of her was disappointed it couldn't play her convincingly. But another part was relieved. If a small model trained on your innermost thoughts can't nail who you are, maybe there is no ground truth to a person. You and I, made of fleeting flesh and bone, are a different kind of thing from narrative fantasy.

She closes with a thirteenth-century Korean legend from the Samguk Yusa. A king with donkey ears. Only his barber knows the shameful secret, so the barber whispers it into a bamboo grove. And forever after, when wind blows through the hollow bamboos, they echo: the king has donkey ears.
We have always been terrified of, and fascinated by, the possibility that things could talk back. Machines promise a world where feelings are an abundant service.
They might also be bamboo groves of capricious magic. That's the line I'll be chewing on all week.
That was Chinese Labs' Latest Product? Roleplay by Irene Zhang, on ChinaTalk. Link in the show notes.
